results.summary: This analog design implements an 8:1 multiplexer that selects one of eight NMOS transistors for characterization, with unselected gates pulled down. Three digital select lines choose the device under test, while bias, drain, and gate voltages are applied through analog pins. Testing requires a source-measure unit to measure drain current and a voltage source to control the selected gate. The project is notable for being a transistor-level performance evaluation block rather than a digital logic design.

This Verilog design generates a VGA video signal to display numbers inspired by the MDR workstations from the TV show Severance. It uses a 25 MHz clock and outputs horizontal and vertical sync along with two bits per color channel. The documentation is minimal, consisting only of a work-in-progress note, so the exact functionality and testing procedure are not described. No external hardware requirements are mentioned beyond a VGA display.

This Verilog project models an enable-controlled PLL clock generator intended for smartcard timing experiments. It accepts a reference clock and provides configuration inputs for feedback divider ratio and charge pump gain, with outputs for the PLL clock, divided clocks, and lock status. The design is verified through cocotb simulation tests that check enable, disable, and lock behavior. No external hardware is required for RTL verification, and the design is notable for exposing internal PLL signals for monitoring.

This Wokwi project implements a simple logic gate simulation where eight input switches feed an AND gate that drives a 7-segment display. Only inputs 5 through 8 produce visible outputs on the display, as the AND gate combines those signals. The design is tested by toggling the input switches and observing the display segments. It requires an external 7-segment display and serves as an introductory educational example.

This Wokwi design demonstrates basic logic gates and clock division, with eight input switches feeding an AND gate and a counter chain. The AND result and two divided clock signals are routed to output pins and a 7-segment display driver. A reset button clears the counter. Testing involves verifying the AND truth table and observing the divided clock outputs on the display.

This Wokwi project implements a 4-bit programmable frequency divider that divides an input clock by a selectable integer N. Four input bits set the division ratio, and the output provides the divided clock. Testing involves applying a low-frequency clock and changing the input bits to observe different output frequencies, preferably with an oscilloscope or a slow clock and LED. The design is a straightforward educational example of clock division.

This Wokwi project implements a simple NAND gate with two inputs and one output. The documentation is essentially a template with placeholder text, providing no details on how the design works or how to test it. No external hardware is mentioned. The project appears to be a minimal logic gate example, but the lack of documentation makes it difficult to assess its purpose or functionality.

This Wokwi project uses simple logic gates to drive a 7-segment display, with four inputs and seven outputs. When all inputs are zero, outputs A through F are high and G is low, displaying the digit 0. The design is tested by setting all inputs to zero and observing the display. It requires an external 7-segment display and serves as an introductory logic exercise.

This Wokwi project displays the reversed word 'sabba' on a 7-segment display using a binary up counter and combinational logic. It runs at a 1 Hz clock, cycling through the letters. Testing involves running the system at 1 Hz and observing the output sequence. The design requires an external 7-segment display and is a simple educational example of counter-driven display patterns.

This Wokwi project uses a NOT gate to display the letter S on a 7-segment display when the input is pressed. The design has one input and one output, with the output being the inverse of the input. Testing involves setting the input to 0 and verifying that the output becomes 1, which lights the appropriate segments for the letter S. It requires an external 7-segment display and is a basic educational example.
